title: The Cyrillic alphabet: familiar shapes and false friends
objectives: I can explain how an alphabet writes sounds, and why a Ukrainian word can be read aloud from its spelling.
I can read the fourteen letters 'а', 'в', 'е', 'и', 'і', 'к', 'м', 'н', 'о', 'р', 'с', 'т', 'у' and 'х' in capital and small form, and say their names.
I can tell the false friends from the English letters they resemble, and say 'в' as [ʋ] before a vowel and [w] where no vowel follows.
I can say the six vowels without gliding, and tell 'и' from 'і', as in 'кит' and 'кіт'.
I can read the stress mark, and read aloud and understand short sentences such as 'Ма́ма тут.' and 'Хто там?'.

vocabulary.note: The everyday word for a mother, used by children and adults alike. Both 'м' are [m] and both 'а' are [ɑ].
Masculine because it names a man, although it ends in '-о' (note 7). The unstressed 'о' keeps its full sound, as the stressed 'а' does.
With family words Ukrainian often leaves out 'my' when it is clear whose relative is meant, where English adds it.
A male cat, or any cat. Ukrainian asks 'хто', 'who', about animals. In the word's other forms, which unit 5 explains, the 'і' becomes 'о': 'кота́'.
The 'н' before 'і' is said with the tongue raised toward the palate (note 4). In the word's other forms, which unit 5 explains, the 'і' becomes 'о': 'но́са'.
One word for both the hand and the whole arm. The 'р' is a tapped or trilled [r], and the 'у' is [u].
The 'в' comes before a vowel, so it is [ʋ], between English 'v' and 'w' (note 3).

example.source: There is a window over there.

vocabulary.note: One word for a city and a town, whatever its size.

example.source: There is a city over there.

vocabulary.note: The drink, and a cup of it. The 'в' comes before a vowel, so it is [ʋ].
Any cheese, and also the fresh curd cheese used in cooking. The 'и' is [ɪ], the 'i' of 'sit'.
The 'с' is [s], never the [k] of 'cat'. In the word's other forms, which unit 5 explains, the 'і' becomes 'о': 'со́ку'.
Any language, and also speech. The 'о' keeps its full, rounded sound, and the 'в' before a vowel is [ʋ].
Above all the traditional whitewashed village house; in everyday speech also a house or a home in general. The 'х' is [x], the 'ch' of 'loch'.
One syllable, so it carries no stress mark (note 6). Both 'т' are said without a puff of air.
Also 'over there'. 'Хто там?' is what Ukrainians call out when someone knocks at the door.
The answer 'yes'. In other sentences the same word means 'so' or 'like this', which later units use.
The answer 'no'. The 'н' before 'і' is said with the tongue raised toward the palate.

example.source: Is the cheese there? No, it is here.

vocabulary.note: Asks about people and also about animals, where English asks 'what'. One syllable: [xtɔ].
Joins words or statements that simply add up.

example.source: There is cheese and juice here.

vocabulary.note: Joins two statements that contrast, with a comma before it, and opens a follow-up question ('А та́то?', 'And Dad?').

example.source: Mom is here, and Dad is there.

grammar.title: Why an alphabet: one letter, one sound
grammar.explanation:
A writing system records a language in signs you can see. Some writing systems give a sign to each word or to each syllable, and need thousands of signs. An alphabet gives a sign, called a letter, to each sound, so a few dozen letters can write every word of the language. Ukrainian is written in its own version of the Cyrillic alphabet, which has 33 letters. The culture note tells where the alphabet comes from.

The principle that makes Ukrainian easy to read is this: each letter stands for one sound, or for a small set of sounds, and when there is a choice, something you can see in the word decides it, such as the letter that follows. English spelling does not work this way: the letters 'ough' are said in different ways in 'though', 'through' and 'tough', so an English reader memorizes many words one by one. Once you know the Ukrainian letters and their few rules, you can sound out almost any word you see, even one you have never met. Only the stressed syllable cannot be read from the spelling, and note 6 explains how this course shows it.

This unit teaches 14 letters: 13 whose shapes look like English letters, and 'и', which looks like a backward 'N'. Unit 2 teaches 13 letters with shapes English does not use, and unit 3 the last six letters and the apostrophe.

The course uses these terms from here on:

- A vowel is a sound made with the air flowing freely through the open mouth, such as the sounds in 'see' and 'father'. Ukrainian has six vowel sounds, and note 4 teaches them.
- A consonant is a sound made by closing or narrowing the mouth somewhere, such as 'm', 's' or 't'.
- A syllable is one beat of a word, built around one vowel sound. 'Ма́ма' has two syllables, 'ма' and 'ма', and 'тут' has one. In Ukrainian you count the syllables of a word by counting its vowel letters.
- In a word of two or more syllables, one syllable is said louder and a little longer than the others: the stressed syllable. The small slanting mark over a vowel, as in 'ма́ма', is the stress mark, which shows that syllable; note 6 explains it.
- Square brackets such as [ɑ] hold symbols of the International Phonetic Alphabet, a system in which each symbol stands for exactly one sound, whatever the language. They let the course be exact. Every sound is also compared with an English sound, so you can rely on the comparisons until the symbols become familiar.

grammar.title: Five familiar letters: 'а', 'к', 'м', 'о', 'т'
grammar.explanation:
Five letters look like English letters and stand for nearly the same sounds: 'а', 'к', 'м', 'о' and 'т'. They are the easy start, but each has a detail that makes your Ukrainian sound right:

- 'а' is [ɑ], the 'a' of 'father', in every word and every syllable. It is never the 'a' of 'cat' or of 'cake'.
- 'о' is [ɔ], said with rounded lips, close to the vowel of 'more' but shorter. It never glides into a 'w' the way the 'o' of 'go' does, and it keeps its full sound when it is not stressed. English weakens an unstressed 'o' to 'uh', as in 'today'; in 'та́то' and 'мі́сто' the last 'о' is as full as the first.
- 'к' is [k] and 'т' is [t], without the puff of air that follows them at the start of English 'kit' and 'top'. Hold a hand in front of your mouth and say 'skin' and 'stop': there is almost no puff, and that is the Ukrainian sound.
- For 'т', the tip of the tongue touches the back of the upper front teeth, a little further forward than for English 't'.
- 'м' is [m], as in 'mom'.

A letter's name is the word you say when you spell aloud, and it is different from the sound the letter makes inside words, just as the English name 'double-u' is not the sound of 'w'. Ukrainian names its letters in two simple ways:

- A vowel letter is named by its sound: 'а' is called 'а', and 'о' is called 'о'.
- A consonant letter is named by its sound with a vowel added: 'к' is 'ка' and 'т' is 'те', with the vowel after it, and 'м' is 'ем', with the vowel before it, like the English name 'em'. The 'е' in these names is [ɛ], the 'e' of 'bed' (note 3).

In the table, Letter gives the capital and the small form, Sound gives the symbol in square brackets, and English gives the nearest English sound. The capitals look exactly like English capitals, but small 'к', 'м' and 'т' are small copies of their capitals, not the English small letters; note 5 shows them.

grammar.title: Eight false friends, and 'и'
grammar.explanation:
A false friend is a letter whose shape matches an English letter but whose sound does not. False friends are the letters that trip English readers, because the eye reads the English letter before the mind catches up. In capitals, 'НІС' looks like English 'HIC', but it is the word 'ніс', nose; 'РУКА́' looks like 'PYKA', but it is 'рука́', hand. Learn each false friend as a new letter that happens to share a shape. The culture note explains why the shapes are shared.

Eight letters of this unit are false friends. A ninth, 'и', is not one, because its shape is not an English letter, but it is taught with them: it looks like a backward 'N', and its sound is easily confused with that of 'і'. The nine letters sound as follows:

- 'в' looks like 'B' and is [ʋ], a sound between English 'v' and 'w': the lower lip comes close to the upper teeth without pressing on them.
- 'е' looks like English 'e' and is [ɛ], the 'e' of 'bed', never the 'ee' of 'me'.
- 'н' looks like 'H' and is [n], the 'n' of 'no'.
- 'р' looks like 'P' and is [r], made with the tip of the tongue tapping once, or trilling a few times, just behind the upper teeth. A single tap is close to the quick 'tt' of American 'better'.
- 'с' looks like 'C' and is [s], the 's' of 'sun', never the [k] of 'cat'.
- 'у' looks like 'y' and is the vowel [u], the 'oo' of 'moon', never the 'y' of 'yes'.
- 'х' looks like 'X' and is [x], the 'ch' of Scottish English 'loch': breath pushed through a narrow gap between the back of the tongue and the roof of the mouth. It is never the 'ks' of 'box'.
- 'и' looks like a backward 'N' and is the vowel [ɪ], the 'i' of 'sit'.
- 'і' looks like English 'i' and is always [i], the 'ee' of 'see', never the 'i' of 'sit' or of 'time'.

'в' is the first letter with a rule you can see. Before a vowel it is [ʋ]: 'вікно́', 'ка́ва'. When no vowel follows it, at the end of a word or before a consonant, it becomes [w], the 'w' of 'cow'. So 'вовк', wolf, is [ʋɔwk]: the first 'в' is followed by 'о', the second by 'к'. The last sound of 'Ха́рків', the city of Kharkiv, is also [w].

The names follow the patterns of note 2. The vowel letters 'е', 'у', 'и' and 'і' are named by their sounds. 'в' is 'ве'; 'н', 'р' and 'с' are 'ен', 'ер' and 'ес', with 'е' first, like 'ем'; and 'х' is 'ха', like 'ка'.

rows: between 'v' and 'w'; 'w' in 'cow' with no vowel after

grammar.title: Six full vowels, and 'и' against 'і'
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian has six vowel sounds, and each has its own letter: 'а', 'о', 'у', 'е', 'и' and 'і'. All six are full and steady: the tongue and lips hold one position from the start of the vowel to its end. Many English vowels glide from one position to another: the 'o' of 'go' ends in a 'w', and the 'a' of 'say' ends in a 'y'. Ukrainian vowels never glide. They also keep their sound when they are not stressed, where English weakens vowels to 'uh', as in the first and last 'a' of 'banana'. Unit 4 teaches one small exception: an unstressed 'е' moves a little toward 'и', as the first vowel of 'сестра́' does, and an unstressed 'и' moves a little toward 'е'.

Two of the six need care, because English writes both sounds with the letter 'i':

- 'и' is [ɪ], the short 'i' of 'sit'.
- 'і' is [i], the 'ee' of 'see', said short and without a glide.

The difference matters, because it can be the only thing that tells two words apart:

- 'кит' [kɪt] means whale.
- 'кіт' [kʲit] means cat.

The pair shows a second difference. A consonant before 'і' is said with the middle of the tongue raised toward the palate, the hard roof of the mouth, as if a 'y' sound were about to begin. So the 'к' of 'кіт' is a little different from the 'к' of 'кит', and the small raised [ʲ] in [kʲit] marks this. With 'н' and 'с' the effect is stronger: listen for it in 'ні', 'ніс' and 'сік'. Before 'и' a consonant stays plain: 'сир' is [sɪr]. Unit 3 names this raised-tongue quality softness and gives its rules.

One more difference helps you read: many Ukrainian words begin with 'і', such as 'і', and, and the name 'Іри́на', but almost none begin with 'и'. 'Іри́на' has both letters: first [i], then [ɪ].

examples.source: Who is here? A whale? No, a cat.

grammar.title: Capital and small letters
grammar.explanation:
Like English, Ukrainian has a capital and a small form of every letter. Capitals are used at the start of a sentence and for the names of people and places, such as 'Окса́на', 'Тара́с' and 'Ха́рків'. Signs and headings are often written all in capitals, so a café sign may read 'КА́ВА'. (Real signs, like all ordinary text, do not print the stress mark that note 6 explains.)

In English the small letters often have shapes quite unlike the capitals, as 'A' and 'a' or 'B' and 'b' do. In Cyrillic most small letters are simply smaller copies of the capitals. This unit's letters fall into two groups:

- 'а', 'е', 'о', 'р', 'с', 'у', 'х' and 'і' have small forms shaped like the English small letters 'a', 'e', 'o', 'p', 'c', 'y', 'x' and 'i'.
- 'в', 'к', 'м', 'н', 'т' and 'и' have small forms that are smaller copies of their capitals, shown in the table.

The second group needs attention when you read. Small 'н' has the shape of a small 'H', with a bar across the middle, so it cannot be confused with English 'n' or 'h'. Small 'т' has the shape of a small 'T', and small 'м' has the pointed shape of a small 'M', not the rounded humps of English 'm'. Small 'в' is a small 'B', not a 'b'. Small 'и' is a small backward 'N'.

Only the size changes: a capital and a small letter are the same letter with the same sound and the same name. Unit 2 shows that italic print and handwriting give a few small letters other shapes.

grammar.title: The stress mark
grammar.explanation:
In a word of two or more syllables, one syllable is said louder and a little longer than the others. It is called the stressed syllable, like 'nan' in English 'banana'. This course marks it with a small slanting line above the vowel of that syllable, the stress mark: 'ма́ма' is stressed on the first syllable, and 'сестра́' and 'вікно́' on the second.

Three facts about the mark are worth knowing:

- It is a teaching aid, not part of the spelling. Ordinary Ukrainian books, signs and messages do not print it; dictionaries and some books for learners do.
- The course writes it on every word of two or more syllables, and never on a word of one syllable, where there is only one syllable to stress: 'кіт', 'тут', 'ніс'.
- When you type an answer, you may leave the mark out; the app ignores it.

The mark matters because Ukrainian stress can fall on any syllable, and the spelling alone does not tell you which: 'ма́ма' is stressed on the first syllable and 'рука́' on the last, although both have two syllables and end in 'а'. Learn the stress together with each word: say the marked syllable louder and longer, and keep the other vowels full, as note 4 says. Unit 4 explains stress in full.

grammar.title: First sentences: 'Ма́ма тут.'
grammar.explanation:
With the words of this unit you can already make whole sentences, because Ukrainian uses no word for 'is' in sentences that say where someone or something is. 'Ма́ма тут.' means 'Mom is here.', word for word 'mom here'. 'Ка́ва там.' means 'The coffee is over there.', word for word 'coffee there'. Ukrainian also has no words for 'a' and 'the', so the English translation supplies them where English needs them. Unit 5 explains both facts. Until then the course shows the word-for-word rendering beside such sentences, so that you see the pattern.

Questions are made in two ways:

- A question with a question word starts with it: 'Хто там?' is 'Who is there?', word for word 'who there?'. 'Хто' asks about people and also about animals: 'Хто там? Кіт.'
- A question without a question word uses the same words as the statement, and the voice rises at the end: 'Ма́ма тут?' means 'Is Mom here?'. The answer begins with 'Так', yes, or 'Ні', no.

Ukrainian has two words for English 'and':

- 'і' simply adds: 'Тут сир і сік.' means 'There is cheese and juice here.'
- 'а' sets two statements against each other, with a comma before it: 'Ма́ма тут, а та́то там.' means 'Mom is here, and Dad is there.' It also opens a follow-up question: 'А та́то?' means 'And Dad?'.

The vocabulary labels each word with its part of speech: the class it belongs to by what it does in a sentence. Unit 5 teaches the classes in full. This unit uses five classes:

- A noun names a person, an animal, a thing or a place: 'ма́ма', 'кіт', 'мі́сто'.
- An adverb adds a fact such as place or time to a sentence: 'тут' and 'там' say where.
- A conjunction joins words or statements: 'і' and 'а'.
- A particle is a short word that adds a meaning to a sentence without naming anything: 'так' and 'ні' answer a question.
- A pronoun stands in place of a noun, and an interrogative pronoun is a pronoun that asks a question: 'хто', who.

Each noun is also labeled masculine, feminine or neuter. These labels name the noun's gender, one of three groups into which Ukrainian sorts its nouns, and the group usually shows in the ending:

- Most masculine nouns end in a consonant: 'кіт', 'сир'.
- Most feminine nouns end in '-а': 'ма́ма', 'ка́ва'.
- Many neuter nouns end in '-о' or '-е': 'вікно́', 'мі́сто'.

'Та́то' ends in '-о' but is masculine, because it names a man. Unit 5 explains what gender does.

examples.source: The cheese is here, and the juice is there.

culture.title: Where the Cyrillic alphabet comes from
culture.text:
The alphabet Ukrainian uses is called Cyrillic, after Saint Cyril, a Byzantine scholar and missionary of the ninth century. Cyril and his brother Methodius made an alphabet for writing a Slavic language, so that Christian books could be read in it. Around the year 900 their followers, working in the First Bulgarian Empire, built a simpler alphabet mostly from the letters of Greek, which was later named after Cyril. It reached Kyiv with Christianity at the end of the tenth century, and Ukrainian has been written in Cyrillic ever since, its letters changing over the centuries to fit the language. Several other languages are also written in versions of Cyrillic, each with its own set of letters; the Ukrainian version has 33.

The false friends of this unit have a simple cause. The Latin alphabet that English uses also descends from the Greek alphabet, by a different route. The two alphabets therefore share many shapes, but over the centuries they came to use some of those shapes for different sounds, and some similar shapes grew out of different Greek letters. So 'Р' and the English 'P', or 'Н' and the English 'H', look alike and stand for different sounds.

Ukrainians mark the Day of Ukrainian Writing and Language every year on November 9. On that day many people across the country, and Ukrainians abroad, take part in a national radio dictation: an announcer reads a text aloud, the listeners write it down, and the text is published afterwards so that everyone can check their spelling. The dictation exercises of this course work the same way.

exercises.explanation: 'н' is a false friend: its shape is 'H', but its sound is [n], as in 'ніс'.

exercises.prompt: What is the name of the letter 'р'?
exercises.explanation: 'р' is named 'ер', with 'е' first, like 'ем', 'ен' and 'ес'.

choices: A small 'H', with a bar across the middle
exercises.explanation: Most small Cyrillic letters are smaller copies of their capitals, so small 'н' is a small 'H'.
'Ма́ма' is mom and 'тут' is here. Dad is 'та́то', and there is 'там'.

exercises.explanation: 'и' is [ɪ]. 'ніс' and 'сік' have 'і', which is [i], the 'ee' of 'see'.

exercises.explanation: 'в' becomes [w] when no vowel follows it. In 'Ха́рків' it ends the word; in the other three a vowel follows it, so it is [ʋ].
'Мі́сто' is a city or a town. A window is 'вікно́', and a house is 'ха́та'.
